newsitem.title: GERMANY: Institutions hedge, individuals cheer as DAX rises.
newsitem.headline: Institutions hedge, individuals cheer as DAX rises.

text.p: The German share market has chalked up record gains most days recently to the delight of investors, but institutions are cautious and have been buying a range of financial tools to hedge against a possible market collapse.
Technical analysts say the market is overbought at current levels and that an 18 percent correction down to 3,600 points is possible without seriously disrupting the long-term upwards trend.

With the market at such heady levels and volumes so high, banks, fund managers and other institutions have been hedging furiously to minimise the downside for both the institutions and the individual investor who has started to invest in funds.
There are fears that Germany's fledgling equity culture could be could dealt a serious blow if a massive correction wipes out the retail investor's hard-earned assets.

Germany's share market has risen around 50 percent this year. The blue-chip DAX index closed bourse trade on Thursday at 4,335.74 points, down 70.35 points, a slight reversal from the record gains of recent weeks.
Opinions differ on whether the market can keep rising at such a rate or whether a huge correction is imminent, but rising volumes in the options market show that market players are taking no chances.

"At the moment there is a noticeable difference between the call ratio on DAX (index) options and the call ratio on (individual) share options," Giro Olbertz, technical analyst at Vereins- und WestBank in Hamburg, said.

A put option is a contract giving the buyer or holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying at an agreed price within a specified time. The seller, or writer, has an obligation to buy.
On Wednesday there were 240,000 put options traded on the DAX index, an increase of 400 percent on the previous day.

A call option on the other hand gives the buyer the right to buy the underlying at an agreed price at or within an agreed time, where the seller, or writer, has the obligation to sell. The put/call ratio is usually used as a sentiment indicator.
A large section of DAX options is in puts, because many institutional investors are hedging using puts at the moment.

"On the other hand, on individual share options there are a lot of calls, because many small investors are reckoning on a rising market, while the institutions are selling share calls, practically using written share calls to finance the purchase of DAX puts," said Olbertz.

"This happens because for the domestic institutions, writing calls is a very popular way of realising extra yields. They usually sell "out-of-the-money" (above the market) calls and get cash up front, which adds liquidity," he said.
Private investors do not usually write calls, because larger holdings of shares are required. Writing options on one or two small contracts is useless, as the costs are high.
"But an institution which can write one or two hundred contracts on a share branch, then this gives volumes which a small investor cannot hope to reach," Olbertz said.
However, Wieland Staud, chief German equities strategist at Yamaichi Bank in Frankfurt, said it is not clear if the small investors stand to make big losses, as the upwards trend is still intact.
"Private investors are more euphoric than institutions. The rise in the market has not yet found its end," said Staud.
A correction of a couple of hundred points is possible in the mid-term based on technicals and on market sentiment.
"If we close around 4,370, we have had a kind of reversal, and we can say the market has taken a short-term breather and could consolidate between 4,100 and 4,400," said Staud.
Olbertz said the market is overbought.

"From a technical point of view this market is overbought and a clear correction is due. But resistance is at 3,600 and at this level the long-term upwards trend is still intact, because the 200-day (moving average) line is at 3,200 points.
"I see 5,000 points as a target level for the market. But as the market is reaching all-time highs practically daily, there are no technical barriers," said Olbertz.
Staud agreed. "I don't believe we've seen the highest point yet -- we could have a fairly heavy consolidation, but the long-term upwards trend is intact."
